Before: Reversible magnesium deposition has been achieved both by weakening ion pairing and by bringing selected anions into the primary solvation shell. This apparent contradiction shows why first-shell composition alone cannot identify the reaction that controls metal transfer. Anion coordination should be judged by its effects on solvent binding, ligand release and competing reduction reactions. These effects can precede, accompany or persist independently of film formation. Representative studies illustrate distinct benefits, including suppression of amine reduction, easier ligand rearrangement and preservation of an active interface. We use these cases to define the evidence that separates population changes, molecular kinetics and retained surface effects. A two-state example distinguishes solvate abundance from reactivity. We then propose controlled experiments and magnesium-specific modelling tests that connect local chemistry to reactions at both electrodes and electrolyte consumption. The aim is to establish reaction pathways that predict electrolyte behaviour beyond the formulations in which they were identified.
After: Strong Mg²⁺–solvent interactions can hinder magnesium deposition, making desolvation a key consideration in electrolyte design. Anions within the first solvation shell can change these interactions and the pathways by which ligands are released. Their contribution therefore extends beyond the formation of an anion-derived solid–electrolyte interphase. In this Perspective, we examine how anion coordination can facilitate Mg²⁺ desolvation and why increased ion pairing is beneficial in some electrolytes but detrimental in others. We discuss how coordination geometry, competing interactions and ligand-exchange dynamics influence the balance between reversible deposition and electrolyte decomposition. Representative studies show the need to distinguish easier ligand release from increased populations of reactive Mg species and improved surface protection. We propose experimental controls and computational approaches to resolve these contributions and establish when a desolvation mechanism applies across electrolyte compositions. Finally, we consider how anion-assisted transfer at the Mg electrode can be reconciled with cathode compatibility and limited electrolyte consumption. This analysis provides a basis for selecting anions that promote desolvation without compromising stability at either electrode.

Before: A working magnesium electrolyte delivers more than dissolved Mg²⁺. It supplies a carrier whose ligands can rearrange, whose reduction produces recoverable metal, and whose reactions leave the surface active. The early rechargeable prototype combined an organohaloaluminate liquid with a Chevrel-phase cathode.[1–2] Earlier and later electrochemical studies established how strongly reversibility depends on donor chemistry and electrode preparation.[3–5] Those dependencies still constrain magnesium and other multivalent batteries.[6–9] The central design question is therefore how a formulation enables magnesium transfer and which features of its mechanism remain useful when the chemistry changes.
After: Reversible magnesium deposition requires an electrolyte that supports ligand rearrangement and Mg reduction without progressively blocking the metal surface. The early rechargeable Mg battery prototype combined an organohaloaluminate electrolyte with a Chevrel-phase cathode.[1–2] Electrochemical studies before and after this demonstration showed that Mg plating/stripping depends strongly on the coordinating solvent and electrode preparation.[3–5] These coupled requirements continue to limit the development of magnesium and other multivalent batteries.[6–9] Understanding how dissolved Mg species undergo desolvation and reduction is therefore essential to improving electrolyte performance beyond a particular formulation.

Before: Lithium provides a useful reference, but magnesium requires a different interpretation of the interface. In lithium electrolytes, salt concentration and anion participation can redirect reduction and improve electrode compatibility.[10–15] A functional lithium SEI limits electronic leakage while allowing ion transport.[16–17] Magnesium often develops blocking films, although selected artificial and electrolyte-derived interfaces sustain cycling.[18–20] Comparative work on Li and Mg emphasizes that the same film-building strategy can have different transport consequences.[21] Identifying a familiar SEI compound is thus less informative than establishing how magnesium passes through the resulting interface.
After: Lithium electrolytes provide useful design principles, but their interphase chemistry cannot be transferred directly to magnesium. In Li systems, salt concentration and anion coordination can alter electrolyte reduction and improve electrode compatibility.[10–15] A functional solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) suppresses electron leakage while permitting Li-ion transport.[16–17] Many decomposition layers on Mg instead inhibit further plating and stripping, although suitable artificial and electrolyte-derived interphases can sustain cycling.[18–20] Comparisons of Li and Mg highlight these different transport requirements.[21] The presence of a familiar SEI component is consequently insufficient to establish that a film supports Mg transport.

Before: The distinction is visible in a hybrid organic/inorganic Mg interphase. A surface formed in its original electrolyte suppresses side reactions after transfer into a TFSI-containing liquid.[20] Part of the benefit therefore resides in the retained surface. Its persistence alone does not establish how ligands leave Mg in the replacement liquid. This experiment illustrates an important distinction: solution coordination constrains the available carriers, while the surface influences how they react. A useful film and an accessible molecular pathway can reinforce one another, but neither establishes the other.
After: A hybrid organic/inorganic Mg interphase illustrates the importance of separating solution chemistry from surface protection. The preformed layer continues to suppress side reactions after the electrode is transferred to a TFSI-containing electrolyte.[20] This observation supports a protective role for the retained interphase, but does not explain how solvated Mg releases its ligands in the replacement electrolyte. Solution coordination influences which Mg species reach the electrode, where their reactions also depend on the evolving surface. Efficient deposition may require both favourable ligand exchange and a permeable, chemically stable interphase; evidence for one does not establish the other.

Before: The divalent charge of Mg generally strengthens its interaction with comparable donors relative to Li, making polarisation, ion association and ligand geometry especially consequential.[22–23] Denticity denotes the number of donor atoms from one ligand bound to the metal; it is not the number of ligand molecules. Anion contact changes carrier charge and geometry while Mg remains formally Mg(II) before reduction. This creates a design paradox. Anion-rich shells can favour interfacial chemistry, yet persistent association can obstruct release. Both strategies have enabled reversible deposition.[24–25] Their success can be reconciled by identifying the reaction step that each coordination environment improves.
After: Compared with Li⁺, Mg²⁺ generally interacts more strongly with similar donor groups, making ligand exchange sensitive to polarisation, ion association and coordination geometry.[22–23] Ligand denticity also matters: one multidentate molecule can bind through several donor atoms. Direct anion coordination changes the charge and geometry of the Mg complex without changing the formal Mg(II) oxidation state. This interaction can favour ligand rearrangement, but persistent Mg–anion binding may impede subsequent release. Reversible deposition has been achieved both by reducing ion pairing and by promoting selected anion–solvent interactions.[24–25] These results raise a mechanistic question: under what conditions does anion coordination facilitate desolvation?

Before: A successful recipe is not yet an explanation. Magnesium electrolytes span organometallic complexes, simple salts and mixed-donor liquids,[26–29] and each substitution changes several processes at once. Coordination number and isolated binding energy describe the starting environment; they do not identify the slow step.[23,30–31] A chloride-complex calculation illustrates the limits of a single descriptor: clustering facilitates calculated desolvation but hinders electron transfer.[32] Chemical equilibria and oxidation introduce further constraints.[33] A descriptor is useful when it predicts a defined response, including a condition under which its apparent advantage disappears.
After: Magnesium electrolytes include organometallic complexes, simple salts and mixtures of coordinating solvents.[26–29] Changing one component can alter ion association, ligand exchange and interfacial reactions simultaneously. Coordination numbers and isolated binding energies describe aspects of the solvation environment, but do not identify the rate-limiting step in deposition.[23,30–31] For example, calculations on chloride-containing Mg complexes suggest that clustering can facilitate desolvation while hindering electron transfer.[32] Chemical equilibria and oxidative stability impose additional constraints.[33] An effective design parameter must therefore describe a specified reaction and predict how that reaction responds to a change in composition or potential.

Before: Mg–solvent, Mg–anion and anion–solvent interactions belong to the same chemical system. Organoboron, non-Grignard and alkoxide electrolytes access different carriers,[34–36] while substituent changes alter the electrochemistry of Grignard-derived formulations.[37] Comparing these families requires a common reaction definition rather than a superficially similar cluster. The relevant information is the populated precursor, its route to the electrode product, and the competing route that consumes electrolyte. Similar Coulombic efficiencies can conceal differences in all three. A transferable design rule should identify which interaction to modify next.
After: The interactions among Mg ions, anions and solvents must be considered together. Organoboron, non-Grignard and alkoxide electrolytes contain chemically distinct Mg species,[34–36] and even changing a substituent can alter the electrochemical behaviour of a Grignard-derived formulation.[37] Comparisons among these families should ask which species participates in deposition, how it loses or rearranges its ligands, and which side reactions compete with Mg reduction. Similar Coulombic efficiencies may arise from different combinations of these processes. Identifying the relevant reaction is what allows a coordination principle established in one electrolyte to guide the design of another.

Before: We propose selecting first-shell anions according to the transfer pathways they enable. An anion can displace a persistent donor, redistribute electron density or create a geometry from which remaining ligands leave more readily. Its contribution can therefore arise before an electrolyte-derived film forms. Studies of competing interactions, dynamic solvation and modulation beyond the primary shell provide complementary starting points.[25,38–39] Here, direct coordination denotes a contact between Mg and an anion donor atom. A contact ion pair contains such a contact; a solvent-separated pair has solvent between the ions. Both remain solvated species.
After: The central argument of this Perspective is that anions in the first solvation shell should be considered for their ability to assist Mg²⁺ desolvation, beyond their possible role as SEI precursors. Anion coordination can change Mg–solvent interactions, displace a strongly bound donor or favour a configuration from which the remaining ligands are more readily released. Such effects can influence deposition before an electrolyte-derived film forms. Studies of competing coordination, dynamic solvation and interactions beyond the first shell provide evidence and hypotheses for these molecular contributions.[25,38–39] Throughout this article, direct coordination means contact between Mg and a donor atom of the anion. A contact ion pair contains this interaction; in a solvent-separated pair, solvent molecules separate the ions.

Before: This Perspective examines how coordination changes transfer, which evidence supports that change, and what happens to the anion. The precursor is the solution or interfacial state populated before the step of interest; it need not be the most stable isolated cluster. Ligand release allows subsequent reactions; decomposition consumes electrolyte and may form a film; persistent binding can trap Mg in an unproductive state. These outcomes demand different measurements. Our test of transferability asks whether a mechanism predicts how a donor, anion or potential change affects Mg transfer in another chemical environment, including its limits.
After: We examine when anion coordination facilitates ligand removal, when it stabilises a slowly reacting Mg complex, and how these effects can be distinguished from interphase formation. A precursor here is a solvated or interfacial Mg species present before the reaction step under consideration. Its abundance, ligand-exchange rate and tendency to decompose require different measurements. Representative electrolytes illustrate these contributions and guide proposed tests at both electrodes. The aim is to connect anion selection with a defined desolvation mechanism and establish whether it remains applicable when the solvent, salt or operating potential changes.

Before: Weak pairing is advantageous when Mg–anion association removes reactive carriers or promotes unwanted chemistry. A solvent-designed Mg(TFSI)₂ formulation combines increased pair dissociation with reversible deposition,[24] whereas earlier TFSI studies show substantial dependence on donor environment and cycling history.[40–42] Reducing anion contact does not remove the need for solvent-shell rearrangement. It shifts attention to solvent rearrangement, carrier supply and the surface reaction. Conductivity and dissociation consequently answer different questions: correlated motion, viscosity and carrier mobility can change the former without producing a corresponding change in molecular release.
After: Weak ion pairing can improve deposition when Mg–anion association limits the supply of reactive Mg species or promotes electrolyte decomposition. A Mg(TFSI)₂ electrolyte designed through solvent selection combines greater ion-pair dissociation with reversible deposition,[24] whereas earlier studies show that TFSI-based electrolytes are sensitive to solvent identity and cycling history.[40–42] Reducing anion coordination, however, leaves the Mg–solvent shell to reorganize before deposition. Solvent exchange and surface reactions can therefore remain limiting even in a well-dissociated electrolyte. Ionic conductivity alone cannot resolve these limitations, because it also depends on viscosity, ion mobility and correlated ion motion.

Before: Weakly coordinating salts approach this problem from the anion side. Boron clusters and carboranes extended Mg chemistry beyond organohalide liquids, with cluster modification addressing solubility and stability.[43–46] Fluorinated borates and alkoxyaluminates added less corrosive and high-voltage options.[47–51] The common design intent is to reduce disruptive association, not to establish identical shells across these chemistries. Even a bulky anion can associate under some conditions. Its practical value rests on whether the remaining donor environment delivers Mg to an active interface.
After: Weakly coordinating anions offer another way to reduce Mg–anion association. Boron clusters and carboranes expanded Mg electrolyte chemistry beyond organohalide formulations, with modification improving solubility and stability.[43–46] Fluorinated borates and alkoxyaluminates provided less corrosive, higher-voltage options.[47–51] Bulky anions can still associate with Mg under suitable conditions. Their usefulness depends on reducing detrimental contacts while allowing the remaining solvent ligands to rearrange at the electrode.

Before: The solvent can become the limitation after persistent anion contacts are reduced. Competitive ethers loosen a borate solvation environment,[52] and hydrofluoroether–diglyme mixtures provide another way to change Mg coordination.[53] Within a controlled series, reduced ion pairing accompanied by slower deposition would redirect the investigation towards solvent departure, adsorption or surface conversion. That response would define the limits of a dissociation-based design rule without invalidating weak pairing as a strategy. The benefit of removing one obstruction depends on the next step in the sequence.
After: After persistent Mg–anion contacts are reduced, solvent coordination may limit desolvation. Competitive ethers can loosen a borate solvation environment,[52] while hydrofluoroether–diglyme mixtures also modify Mg coordination.[53] If ion pairing decreases but deposition slows within a controlled series, measurements of solvent exchange, adsorption and surface reactions can identify the remaining constraint. This comparison establishes when further dissociation ceases to improve deposition.

Before: A direct carborane–TFSI comparison is particularly useful because it examines the Mg/electrolyte interface alongside anion identity.[54] Initial shell assignments alone miss the chemical divergence that develops during cycling. Measurements of recovered Mg, soluble products and surface evolution reveal where the pathways diverge. Before: Chloride electrolytes demonstrate that direct anion coordination is compatible with Mg transfer. Structural studies identify chloride-containing carriers with coordination and charge unlike a solvent-only Mg²⁺ solvate.[55–60] Magnesium/aluminium speciation, donor choice and conditioning determine their electrochemical behaviour.[61–67] Chloride can act within the approaching complex and at the surface. After: Chloride-based electrolytes show that direct anion coordination can be compatible with reversible Mg deposition. Structural studies identify chloride-containing Mg complexes whose charge and coordination differ from those of solvent-only Mg²⁺ solvates.[55–60] Their electrochemical behaviour depends on Mg/Al speciation, solvent identity and conditioning.[61–67] Chloride can participate in the solvated complex and influence the electrode surface. Because these functions are coupled, neither complete anion exclusion nor the largest possible contact-ion-pair fraction provides a general design rule. The relevant question is how coordination affects the individual steps leading to Mg deposition.

Before: The amine example identifies one specific benefit of primary-shell pairing. Weakened amine coordination suppresses reduction and H₂ evolution, with 99.6% CE reported for 800 cycles.[80] This result establishes improved reversibility and supports suppression of side reactions. The competing solvent–anion study instead proposes synchronous ligand release and reports 0.06 V reduction overpotential at 1 mA cm⁻² together with an MgH₂-containing interphase.[25] The molecular and surface contributions remain coupled. The protocols differ and cannot establish a kinetic ranking. In particular, identifying MgH₂ does not determine which phase, boundary or defect transports Mg through the operating film.
After: Amine-containing electrolytes illustrate how first-shell anion coordination can improve reversibility without establishing faster desolvation as the sole cause. In one study, weakened amine coordination suppresses amine reduction and H₂ evolution, with a reported Coulombic efficiency (CE) of 99.6% for 800 cycles.[80] Another study proposes that competition between solvent and anion coordination enables synchronous ligand release; it reports a reduction overpotential of 0.06 V at 1 mA cm⁻² and an MgH₂-containing interphase.[25] In the latter case, molecular and interphase effects both require consideration. The different protocols prevent a direct kinetic comparison. Moreover, detecting MgH₂ does not establish which phase, interface or defect carries Mg through the operating interphase.

After: Chelating anions provide a further example. MgEDTF is magnesium (1R,2R)-1,2-diphenylethane-1,2-diylbis(trifluoromethylsulfonylamide), whose EDTF²⁻ anion forms a coordinatively unsaturated Mg–anion–DME complex.[81] The reported plating/stripping overpotential decreases from 2.0 to 0.24 V relative to the non-chelating analogue, with a substantial contribution attributed to the anion-derived SEI. Before: Table 1 translates these reports into mechanistic choices. Dissociation is the appropriate target when association restricts carrier availability. Ligand departure becomes the target when donors persist, and selectivity or surface activation becomes the target when charge is lost to decomposition. Dissociation can increase the supply of reactive Mg species; ligand removal, suppression of decomposition and interphase modification address other limitations. The published results instead identify mechanistic questions for controlled electrolyte series.

Before: First-shell occupancy measures association; transfer requires a route out of that associated state. An abundant precursor can feed deposition, exchange slowly or undergo decomposition.[23,30–31] Its abundance alone gives no ordering of those outcomes. The activation barrier is referenced to the state populated under operating conditions. Stabilizing this state more than the transition state raises the barrier, even if both absolute energies decrease. Figure 2 illustrates why the energetic benefit of an anion depends on the relative stabilisation along the pathway, not on the energy of a single isolated cluster.
After: The prevalence of Mg–anion contacts describes the coordination environment, but not how readily the resulting complexes react. An abundant Mg species may undergo rapid ligand exchange, remain kinetically stable or decompose during reduction.[23,30–31] The relevant activation barrier is the free-energy difference between the populated initial state and the transition state. If coordination stabilises the initial state more strongly than the transition state, the barrier increases even though both states decrease in absolute energy. Figure 2 illustrates why a low energy for an isolated Mg complex does not, by itself, demonstrate easier desolvation.

Computed partial charges depend on the electronic model, whereas the formal Mg oxidation state remains unchanged by binding. After: Anion coordination can alter Mg–solvent binding by changing electron distribution and coordination geometry, without weakening every interaction in the complex. Computed partial charges depend on the electronic-structure model and should be distinguished from the formal Mg oxidation state. Interactions between anions and solvents can also change the Mg species present without requiring every cosolvent to enter the first shell.[82–84] For example, the solvent–anion “counterpoised” strategy proposes that competition for Mg coordination facilitates ligand release.[25] Studies of weak solvent–solvent interactions provide further context for effects originating in the surrounding liquid.[85]

Before: An energy comparison begins with a balanced chemical reaction. Ion-pairing free energy compares associated and dissociated states in a specified liquid. Exchange free energy compares a bound donor, its replacement and the released donor. An activation barrier concerns the intervening transition state. Charge, solvent activity, composition and reference conditions give each quantity its meaning. Association can change carrier populations and subsequent reactivity.[23,32] A deeper precursor minimum does not by itself imply a lower escape barrier. Treating association energy as a release barrier obscures the competition between precursor stabilisation and release that electrolyte design needs to resolve.
After: To establish whether anion coordination facilitates desolvation, the relevant free energies must be distinguished. Ion-pairing free energy describes the equilibrium between associated and dissociated ions. Ligand-exchange free energy compares states before and after one ligand replaces another. The activation barrier is the free-energy difference between the initial and transition states. Each calculation requires a balanced reaction with specified charge, solvent activity, composition and reference conditions. Association changes Mg-complex populations and reactivity.[23,32] Stabilising a complex can nevertheless raise its release barrier if the transition state is stabilised less. Association energy alone therefore cannot establish that an anion assists desolvation.
